planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; John's Lucifer, registered by John C. Taylor in 1986, is documented chiefly as a Louisiana iris breeding parent, and like other Louisiana iris it thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil.

directions: John's Lucifer is a Louisiana iris cultivar registered by John C. Taylor in 1986, documented in breeding records as a parent crossed with 'Jeri' by Joseph Mertzweiller to produce the 1990-registered cultivar 'Aunt Shirley'. It shares the broad, flat-faced flower form and vigorous, spreading rhizome habit typical of Louisiana iris hybrids. Grow it in full sun with consistently wet to moist, fertile, slightly acidic soil, and divide congested clumps every four to five years in late summer to maintain vigor.

common_name: Shining Tot Hosta (Parent of Shiny Penny)

planting.note: Plant divisions in early fall or spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Shining Tot (P. Aden, 1982, a Hosta venusta x 'Rock Master' cross) is documented chiefly as a hosta breeding parent.

directions: Shining Tot is a hosta cultivar whose main documented legacy is as a breeding parent: Bob Solberg of Green Hill Farm crossed it with 'Lemon Lime' to produce the miniature gold-leaved Shiny Penny, registered in 1997. Like other hostas it forms a clump of foliage from a crown that spreads slowly by offsets rather than running stolons, and performs best in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Plant divisions in early fall or spring, keeping soil consistently moist through summer heat, and mulch to conserve moisture and protect the crown over winter.

common_name: Jane Phillips Bearded Iris (Parent of Eleanor's Pride)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; Jane Phillips is documented chiefly as a bearded iris breeding parent.

directions: Jane Phillips is a bearded iris cultivar whose main documented legacy is as a breeding parent: Edward Watkins crossed it with 'Blue Rhythm' to produce Eleanor's Pride, the powder-blue tricolor-blooming iris that went on to win the American Dykes Medal in 1961. Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun, never buried, in well-drained soil, since standing moisture causes rot far more readily than this iris is troubled by drought. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom, discarding the old woody center and replanting only firm, healthy fans.

common_name: Tressie Cook Louisiana Iris (Grandparent of Charlie's Ginny)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Tressie Cook is documented chiefly as a Louisiana iris breeding parent, and like other Louisiana iris it thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil.

directions: Tressie Cook is a Louisiana iris cultivar whose main documented legacy is as a breeding parent: Charles W. Arny Jr. crossed it with 'W. B. MacMillan', and in turn crossed that seedling with 'Louise Arny', to produce Charlie's Ginny, a bright rose bitone registered in 1972 that went on to parent later bitone-breeding lines. It shares the broad, flat-faced flower form and spreading rhizome habit typical of Louisiana iris hybrids. Grow it in full sun with consistently wet to moist, fertile, slightly acidic soil, and divide congested clumps every four to five years in late summer to maintain vigor.

common_name: Fiesta Gal Louisiana Iris (Bitone Breeding-Line Descendant of Charlie's Ginny)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Fiesta Gal is documented as part of the bitone-breeding line descending from 'Charlie's Ginny', and like other Louisiana iris it thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil.

directions: Fiesta Gal is a bitone Louisiana iris documented as part of the breeding line descending from Charlie's Ginny, named alongside the white-and-green 'Helen Naish' as one of the later cultivars carrying forward Charlie's Ginny's bitone coloring. It shares the broad, flat-faced flower form and vigorous, spreading rhizome habit typical of Louisiana iris hybrids. Grow it in full sun with consistently moist to wet soil through the bloom period, and divide crowded clumps after flowering to maintain vigor.
